newsitem.title: FRANCE: French financial markets recover their nerve - MAY 27.
newsitem.headline: French financial markets recover their nerve - MAY 27.

text.p: French investors recovered their nerve Tuesday after Monday's selling wave, betting that even if the left won the parliamentary election, there would be no radical change in economic policy.

The blue-chip CAC 40 index closed up nearly one percent after plunging 3.9 percent Monday -- its biggest one-day dive in four years -- following the left's upset victory in the first legislative round Sunday. Bonds also steadied but the franc retraced its gains in late trade on foreign selling pressure.

Financial analysts said they did not believe plans by France's unpopular prime minister, Alain Juppe, to resign would give a big boost to the center-right's re-election chances in the final vote next Sunday, saying this smacked too much of panic.
But "people figure even if it is the left in power, they will have to follow the discipline imposed by world financial markets," one share analyst said.

"There's what they (the Socialists) say and there is the reality. And the reality is they do not have much money in the public coffers," said another analyst. "The margin for maneuver is very slim for the left as for the right."

The CAC-40 index slid 0.71 percent at the open but retraced its losses to close up 0.96 percent or 25.60 points at 2,680.34 in concert with other European markets which defied Wall Street weakness to end higher.
Fears the Bourse could be in for another hammering after traders in New York and London returned to their desks following a long holiday weekend did not materialise.
"The surprise is U.S. investors have not sold. They're still betting on a center-right victory Sunday," a broker said.
The Socialists moved late Monday to persuade voters a Socialist-led administration would govern responsibly, pledging no rises in income taxes or public spending.
Shares in defense electronics firm Thomson-CSF rose 2.16 percent to 175.0 francs after plunging 9.6 percent Monday amid fears the Socialists could scrap its privatisation.
Other privatisation stocks also recovered, such as bank Credit Lyonnais, which jumped 7.66 percent to 229.0 francs.

"There were fears privatisation would have to be stopped but there is a growing realisation a Socialist-led government will also have to sell shares," a trader said. "They will need it for their budget."

The franc rallied from Monday's low of 3.3784 against the German currency to hit 3.3746 per mark but then fell back late in the day to 3.3766. A Paris trader said foreign dealers were seeing if they could drive down the franc but that the Bank of France was likely to intervene to prevent any attack.
Bond and interest futures rose on Juppe's resignation plans announced Monday night after the markets closed but selling by non-resident investors knocked them from their highs.

The June bond future contract settled 16 basis points higher at 128.46, after plunging 68 points Monday. The yield premium on 10-year government bonds against their German counterparts was steady at minus 10. It was minus 14 before Sunday's vote.
Bond analysts said the market would likely continue to be supported by domestic investors who took advantage of the rise in yields after the first round vote to buy along the curve.
Hampered by restrictions on overseas investing and hungry for yield, French domestic financial institutions traditionally step in whenever the bond market drops.

Dominique Barbet, bond analyst at Banques Paribas, said domestic investors expected France to continue trimming public deficits and to remain committed for the timetable for a single European currency, no matter which party came to power.

President Jacques Chirac, whose bid to win a free hand in the run-up to monetary union has gone badly awry, was due to address the country in an evening televised speech. But analysts were sceptical he could salvage the center-right's chances.

Juppe's decision to quit was "a step in the right direction but far too late. It emphasises the disarray. Why is Juppe unpopular? Not because he's a horrible man but because of the measures the government introduced," said BZW's Phyllis Reed.
